title: Rosh Hashanah
hook: the Jewish new year, with the shofar and apples in honey; Hannah pours out her soul at Shiloh, then goes her way and eats
tomorrow: Nanak's father gave him money for a good deal. what did he buy?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: eid mubarak. On Eid, the feast begins with food given away so everyone can join. Today, another new year, with honey on the table.

A first Rosh Hashanah dinner can puzzle a guest: the day is called a day of judgment, and the table is full of honey. Jewish tradition reads a story on the first morning that helps. Year after year, a woman named Hannah goes up with her family to the house of God at Shiloh, and year after year she comes home without the child she longs for. This year she weeps and won't eat. She goes to pray, her lips moving, no sound coming out. The old priest Eli watches her, and decides she is drunk.
screen: `JUDGMENT, AND HONEY.` → `HANNAH AT SHILOH.` → `LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` → `ELI THINKS SHE'S DRUNK.`

segments.voice: How long wilt thou be drunken? Eli asks. And Hannah answers: "I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD." Eli sends her away in peace. Then comes a small line, easy to miss: "So the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad." Nothing has changed yet. She has only been heard. Later the text says "the LORD remembered her," and she has a son, Samuel, the boy who would one day hear his name in the night. This is why Jews read her story on this day. The Torah calls the first day of the seventh month "a memorial of blowing of trumpets," a day of remembering, and the Talmud says that on Rosh Hashanah, Hannah was remembered. So Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year, holds both: the shofar, the ram's horn, sounds over a day of judgment, and the prayers ask God to remember. And the table is sweet: apples in honey, round challah, the wish for a good and sweet year. Pour out the heart, then go and eat. Now a neighbor's story. The Qur'an tells of another mother, the wife of Imran, who vows the child she is carrying to God's service, as Hannah vowed Samuel. Her child is Mary. The shared thing: a mother's prayer, heard. And an honest difference: Hannah prays for a child she doesn't have yet, and her story is read on a day Jews keep each year; the Qur'an's mother offers a child already on the way, and the story turns to Mary.
screen: `POURED OUT MY SOUL BEFORE THE LORD.` · `SHE WENT HER WAY, AND DID EAT.` · `A MEMORIAL: A DAY OF REMEMBERING.` · `A MOTHER'S PRAYER, HEARD.` · then, large: `A SWEET YEAR.`

segments.voice: If there's something sweet nearby, honey, fruit, a square of chocolate, hold a small piece and don't eat it yet. Name, silently, one thing you'd ask to be remembered for this year. Then take the bite, and taste it slowly, the way Hannah went her way and ate.
Rosh Hashanah: the head of the year, the Jewish new year, with the shofar's call and apples in honey for a sweet year.
Something to hold: a sweet year, after a heart poured out and heard. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah Jews gather in synagogue to hear the shofar; on the first day the reading from the Prophets is Hannah's story (1 Samuel 1-2). At home they eat apples dipped in honey and round challah with the wish for a good and sweet year; the day begins the Days of Awe that lead to Yom Kippur.

Unity thread: Jesus's 'when thou makest a feast, call the poor' (Luke 14:13) shares the idea that a holy feast reaches those with nothing.
